en_summary: @aleabitoreddit argues that after the Lumentum/$MRVL deal, independent Western laser names $AAOI, $COHR and $SIVE became more strategically valuable, with $MTSI and $SMTC also in focus for 2027, while $AMD and others may rethink reliance on $LITE and chase vertical integration. $MRVL is framed as setting an M&A precedent rather than a fresh buy call.
text:
Following the Lumentum / Marvell deal: 

My opinion is that independent Western laser players, like $AAOI, $COHR, and $SIVE became a lot more strategically valuable. 

$MTSI and $SMTC should get some attention too as emerging laser players in 2027. 

If I had to guess: 

1. Companies competing against Marvell, or not in the $NVDA ecosystem bandwagon, such as $AMD, are likely going to rethink their relationship with $LITE.

If getting bottlenecked by Nvidia capacity agreements wasn't enough... Incentives around qualifying + bringing up other laser players, seems very necessary now. 

Since you generally don't want competitors like Marvell to have influence or visibility over your roadmaps, IP, capacity, pricing, etc. even if there is a "firewall".  

2. $MRVL acquiring Lumentum opened pandoras box in a way of acquiring a critical chokepoint all your competitors + buyers use. 

$LITE was used by your major hyperscalers and across AI supply chains. 

Now, your leaders might wonder if weaponizing capacity agreements might not be as effective.... If someone else can just buy the entire company. 

There's only a few major public merchant Western players out there, and I'm also sure many others will want to follow the Marvell / Broadcom route via vertical integration, given I think $MRVL saves around $1B+ in costs/year. 

So M&A premiums likely went up. 

$SMTC was actively looking to buy laser capacity via M&A so I'm sure they're looking at $SIVE given their 100M CW DFB laser expan

text:
Is 2027 the year of agentic finance?

Base's Jesse Pollak says his AI agents now run his books, budget, and trades, and even find him yields he never had time to access

"They're getting big and growing. Still small in the grand scheme of overall payments volume, but we definitely are seeing growth on Base."

"All of these are going to be doing payments on behalf of people, and so I expect it to grow very quickly."

"I think 2026 is kind of the year where agentic payments emerge. My sense is that 2027 is going to be the year where agentic finance really emerges."

"We're seeing the early signs of this already. People using these agents to manage their whole financial life. And I've actually moved to doing this entirely."

"My agents are now doing all of my bookkeeping, all of my accounting, all of my budgeting. They're telling me about my investments. They're letting me trade on Coinbase."

"They're letting me do things in terms of accessing yield that I wasn't really able to do before, because I just didn't have the time."

en_summary: In the Netherlands, employers must continue paying sick employees for 728 days, nearly two years, compared to 77 days in Luxembourg, a gap of 651 days. This puts Dutch companies at a significant competitive disadvantage.
text:
Hello Monday!

This chart has been circulating on my timeline for the past couple of days.

In the Netherlands, employers are required to continue paying sick employees for 728 days. Almost TWO YEARS!

Second is Luxembourg, with just 77 days. A gap of 651 days!

Protecting sick employees is commendable and understandable. Sometimes things don't go your way.

But why put Dutch companies at such an enormous competitive disadvantage?

Sure, every country has its own system, so a one-to-one comparison isn't entirely fair. But a gap this extreme is hard to justify.

Why would any country choose this?

en_summary: Base's Jesse Pollak says crypto mainstream adoption means less than 1% of the world's dollars and equities are onchain so far, with clear product-market fit and growth but not yet pumping bags. He expects the share to rise from under 1% to 10%, 50%, 90% over the next 5-10 years as major financial companies adopt for faster, cheaper services.
text:
Crypto is taking off. So why aren't bags pumping?

Base's Jesse Pollak says this is what mainstream adoption looks like, with less than 1% of the world's dollars and equities onchain

"There's almost like a weird feeling at times in crypto over the last year, where I think people feel almost a dissonance of like, oh my god, it's so clear that we're taking off from a product market fit and growth perspective, but maybe this isn't what we expected, and maybe it's not pumping our bags."

"The way I look at this is, this is what mainstream adoption looks and feels like."

"When you have a technology that is getting adopted by the biggest financial companies in the world because it offers faster, cheaper, better financial services, I think that's the vision that we've been building towards now for 13 years."

"Look at stablecoins or look at equities. We have less than 1% of the world's dollars, less than 1% of the world's equities moving on these new rails."

"Over the next 5 years, 10 years, it's going to be about going from less than 1% to 10% to 50% to 90%, and that is just a massive, massive pie."

US healthcare costs are rising at an alarming rate:

Medical care prices have surged +132% since 2000, the largest increase among major consumer spending categories.

Over the same period, shelter costs have risen +127%, while food prices have soared +112%.

Price increases across all these spending categories have outpaced overall CPI, which is up +99% since 2000.

As a result, ~30% of insured US adults have skipped or delayed getting healthcare they needed due to costs over the last 12 months, according to a KFF survey.

Healthcare costs have never been higher.

text:
I think AI compute cost-per-watt prices are going to stay elevated a lot longer than many people expect.

Less than 5% of U.S. consumers even pay a subscription for an AI product, with some putting the estimate <2%. People are clearly finding Grok Bot to be very useful because @SpaceX just had to significantly cut back usage capacity due to overwhelming demand. But we're still so early in the AI adoption curve.

Existing users are going to eat up significantly more compute as models get better and agents start handling increasingly complex tasks and jobs. Inference will increasingly become a larger and larger share of compute capacity.

People are seriously underestimating how much demand is still ahead of us and how long it'll take supply to catch up. I think this is partly why Elon thinks SpaceX could exit 2027 with an annual recurring revenue rate of $500 billion to $1 trillion. They can deploy the compute faster than anyone else, and the demand for that compute is insatiable, and likely will be for a long time to come.
